read: partial: abstract, sections 1-5 (introduction, methodology, results, related work, discussion) and appendices A, B, C, F and G in full; appendices D (error examples) and E (unsolved questions) not read beyond their headings
venue_now: not stated in the text; arXiv 2609.13009v1 [cs.AI], 11 Sep 2026 (p.1 stamp)
what_it_is: An expert audit of six physics benchmarks (UGPhysics, PHYBench, PRISM-Physics, HLE-Physics, CMT-Benchmark, CritPt), limited to text-only questions with verifiable final answers, plus a re-scoring of three frontier models before and after correction (p.1, p.3). Experts sort each rejected answer into model error, grader error or benchmark error (p.3-4). The pooled attribution covers 250 questions that one model (GPT-5.6-Sol, High effort) had rejected in the audit runs, out of 502 questions in four benchmark subsets: HLE-Physics 98 rejected, PHYBench 56, PRISM-Physics 74, UGPhysics 22 (p.11, p.13). After conflict resolution, 143 are benchmark errors, 95 grader errors and 12 model errors (p.13). CMT-Benchmark and CritPt are audited separately, by repairing or excluding flawed questions, and corrected scores rise sharply (p.5-6, p.12).
domain: physics, from undergraduate to research level (condensed matter theory in CMT-Benchmark, frontier research in CritPt); no engineering (p.1, p.3)
size: six benchmarks and three models (p.3); pooled audit of 502 questions, 250 rejected and reviewed (p.13), drawn from 100-question subsets of PHYBench, PRISM-Physics and UGPhysics and the 202 text-only HLE-Physics questions (p.11-12); CMT-Benchmark 50 questions and CritPt 56 of 71 audited in full (p.12); 446 reviewer annotations on the 250 rejections (p.18)
source_of_items: existing benchmarks, audited and not built: exercises and exams (PHYBench, PRISM-Physics, UGPhysics) and expert-authored questions (HLE-Physics, CMT-Benchmark, CritPt) (p.3)
instances: static (existing benchmark items; the audit repairs or excludes defective ones) (p.3-4)
has_gold_traces: no: reference final answers only, with worked solutions for some benchmarks; only the final answer is scored, and PRISM-Physics's process-level evaluation is not used (p.3)
evaluation: final answer. Before the audit, each benchmark's own evaluator: rule-based for PHYBench and PRISM-Physics (p.4), a SymPy evaluator with an optional LLM judge for UGPhysics (p.11). After the audit, one LLM-judge pipeline adapted from HLE for every corrected score (p.3-4). No step-level scoring.
human_validation: Experts audit the benchmarks and their graders; they do not label reasoning steps. The 250 rejected questions were reviewed by physics PhD students who saw the question, the reference solution, the model response and an AI-generated preliminary review; 196 questions had two reviewers and 54 had one; the two labels differed on 56 of the 196 (28.57%) and a third review settled all 56 (p.18). Most conflicts were benchmark-versus-grader (34) and benchmark-versus-model (19); grader-versus-model were 3 (p.19). For CritPt and CMT-Benchmark one specialist per problem repaired or excluded it and supplied the reference solution (p.12, p.17). The HLE-adapted LLM judge had the lowest grader-error rate of the evaluators audited, 4.08% (p.4).
contamination_measures: none of its own; it separates public-source benchmarks, open to training-data contamination, from expert-authored ones and focuses its analysis on the latter (p.3-4)

engtrace_use.sentence: Graders themselves can fail: physicists re-grading 250 answers marked wrong on four physics benchmarks attributed all but 12 of them to errors in the benchmark or the grader (Ansari et al., 2026). [marked cut first in v3]
engtrace_use.explanation: All the numbers check; the wording is loose in four places. Numbers: 250 rejected questions (HLE-Physics 98, PHYBench 56, PRISM-Physics 74, UGPhysics 22; 98+56+74+22 = 250) (p.11, p.13); 143 benchmark errors (57.20%), 95 grader errors (38.00%) and 12 model errors (4.80%), so 238 of 250 (95.20%) are benchmark or grader errors (p.13); by benchmark, benchmark/grader/model is 86/4/8 (HLE-Physics), 13/40/3 (PHYBench), 26/48/0 (PRISM-Physics) and 18/3/1 (UGPhysics), and rows and columns add up (p.13). The paper puts it as 'an expert audit of 250 cases across four benchmark subsets, in which expert review attributes 12 to the model. The other 238 are defects in the questions or the graders' (p.8). There is no other category: three labels, one per case (p.3-4, p.18). Loose wording. (1) 'four physics benchmarks' are four benchmark subsets of the six audited (100-question samples of PHYBench, PRISM-Physics and UGPhysics, and the 202 text-only HLE-Physics questions); CMT-Benchmark and CritPt are outside the pooled attribution (p.11-13). (2) '250 answers marked wrong' are 250 questions whose single stored answer, from one model (GPT-5.6-Sol at High effort), was rejected on every attempt (up to five for HLE-Physics and PHYBench, one for PRISM-Physics and UGPhysics) (p.12); they are not a random sample of wrong answers, and the paper says the counts are not a reconstruction of its scores (p.13). (3) 'physicists' were physics PhD students who also saw an AI-generated preliminary review; faculty advised and endorsed them (p.18-19); 54 of the 250 had one reviewer, and the two labels differed on 28.57% of double-reviewed questions before a third review (p.18). (4) 'errors in the benchmark or the grader': defective questions or reference solutions, which include ambiguity and missing assumptions (p.3), are the larger share (143 against 95), and the grader errors sit mainly with rule-based evaluators, 88 of 95 on PHYBench and PRISM-Physics (p.4, p.13), against 4 of 98 for the LLM-judge pipeline on HLE-Physics (p.4, p.13). The lead clause 'Graders themselves can fail' is supported, but chiefly for rule-based graders.

suggested_wording: Graders can fail too: in an expert audit of 250 answers that one model got wrong on four physics benchmark subsets, 95 were correct answers rejected by the benchmark's grader, mostly rule-based expression matching, and 143 came from defective questions or reference solutions; only 12 were model errors (Ansari et al., 2026).
facts_to_cite: six benchmarks audited; the pooled attribution covers four subsets: 502 questions, of which 250 were rejected by one model (GPT-5.6-Sol, High effort) and reviewed: HLE-Physics 98, PHYBench 56, PRISM-Physics 74, UGPhysics 22 (p.11-13)
after conflict resolution: 143 benchmark errors (57.20%), 95 grader errors (38.00%), 12 model errors (4.80%); 238 of 250 (95.20%) are benchmark or grader errors (p.13)
benchmark/grader/model errors by benchmark: HLE-Physics 86/4/8, PHYBench 13/40/3, PRISM-Physics 26/48/0, UGPhysics 18/3/1 (p.13)
grader errors concentrate in rule-based evaluators: 88 of the 95 are on PHYBench and PRISM-Physics (p.4, p.13); the HLE-adapted LLM-judge pipeline had the lowest grader-error rate, 4.08% (p.4)

definitions: model error = well-posed problem and correct reference but wrong model answer; grader error = correct model answer marked wrong; benchmark error = incorrect reference, inconsistent conditions, ambiguity or a missing assumption; one label per case, and benchmark error takes precedence (p.3-4, p.18)

reviewers were physics PhD students who saw the question, the reference solution, the model response and an AI-generated preliminary review; 196 questions had two reviewers and 54 one; 56 of 196 pairs (28.57%) disagreed and a third review resolved all of them (p.18)
the audited answers come from one model, GPT-5.6-Sol at High effort, rejected on every one of up to five attempts (HLE-Physics, PHYBench) or on a single attempt (PRISM-Physics, UGPhysics) (p.12)
subsets: PHYBench 100 of 500 (those with public solutions), PRISM-Physics 100 sampled from 833 text-only questions, UGPhysics 100 sampled from 5,520, HLE-Physics 202 text-only of 230 (p.11)
scoring is by final answer only; PRISM-Physics's process-level evaluation is not used (p.3)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the concern that the scorer itself can be wrong, tested by expert review of the scorer's decisions, and a three-way split of error sources (model, grader, benchmark). Lacks: step-level scoring (final answers only, p.3); generated instances (static benchmark items, p.3); gold reasoning traces (reference answers and, for some benchmarks, worked solutions, p.3); an engineering domain (physics only); step-level expert labels (the expert labels are three-way attributions of rejected final answers, p.18). The positioning claim still holds. What EngTrace adds: generated instances across five engineering branches, deterministic checks of intermediate values against code-computed gold traces, and an evaluator validated against step labels from 15 experts.
notes: (1) Venue is not stated in the text; only the arXiv stamp appears. (2) The audit design (answers rejected on every attempt by one model) shows how rejected answers divide between model, grader and benchmark, not how often graders err overall. (3) The only sentence about this paper is marked cut first. If it is cut nothing in the positioning claim is lost, and the rule-based-checker point is already made by Huang et al. (2026) in the evaluator paragraph. A shorter version if it stays: 'Graders can fail too: of 250 rejected answers on four physics benchmark subsets, experts found 95 to be correct answers that a grader marked wrong (Ansari et al., 2026).' (4) Inference, not in the paper: wrong reference answers, the largest category here, should not arise where the template code is correct, but ambiguous wording can; the paper counts ambiguity and missing assumptions as benchmark errors (p.3). (5) The note added on p.8 reports a separate expert correction of CritPt by another group (31 of 71 problem statements revised), consistent with this paper's CritPt result.
